Matty Wegehaupt · Neenah Club · October 19, 2026

Spoken argument · 2 minutes

Getting Korea Right, Getting Ourselves Right, Getting the World Right.

My objective is simple: the next time you see Korea in the news, you’ll have a better framework of understanding. You’ll be ready for Second Grade material.

My own connections include UW–Madison, a Fulbright in Korea, translating Korean Buddhist teachers, and teaching at Lawrence in Appleton since 2007. Before that, two years at the Air Force Academy. My Korean name is 오상진, Oh Sangjin. Listening to Koreans in their own language has changed how I understand both Korea and America.

Let’s begin with a little Korean. 안녕하세요. Annyeonghaseyo. Hello. This letter is ㄹ, rieul. Listen to it in 우리, uri, and 사랑, sarang. Try those with me: 우리. 사랑.

In these words, the tongue makes a quick tap behind the upper teeth. Listen to the sound rather than making it into the English r. 우리 means we or our. 사랑 means love. Two familiar ideas, in a language that may be new to us.

That gives us our outline. Getting Korea Right: the language, the people, 한국 and 조선. Getting Ourselves Right: 미국—our history of war, diplomacy, and alliance. Getting the World Right: Korea at the center, shaping global industry, culture, and security. That reaches all the way to Wisconsin. 정, and finally 인연. Inyeon.

We have already begun listening to Korea on its own terms. Now let’s bring out the Korea we already carry in our heads.

Opening transition · delivery and image sources

Begin with the familiar nighttime view of the Korean Peninsula. Advance once to dissolve into equal-size photographs of Pyongyang and Seoul. The exact title remains fixed. Advance again to reach the audience-association slide. Left arrow returns to the night view. The reveal is controlled by the speaker, not a timer.

The user requested a satellite contrast followed by paired images of prosperity in DPRK and ROK. Keep the original orbital photograph continuous: its bright upper-left area is China, the dark center is North Korea, and the bright lower-right area is South Korea. A left/right cut down the photograph’s center would misidentify China. The second view is a 50/50 pairing of the two Korean cities.

The photographs show visible urban development in both capitals. They are not evidence of a joint development project, equal national incomes, or living conditions throughout either country. The satellite photograph records nighttime illumination in 2014, not a current welfare survey. Let the visual contrast introduce the argument without adding another claim or question to the slide.

  • NASA: Korean Peninsula seen from the Space Station. Expedition 38 crew; ISS038-E-038300; captured January 30, 2014. NASA article published February 24, 2014. Displayed as an intact photograph.
  • Previous title image: Yonhap: KCNA Pyongyang photograph carried February 17, 2026. The publisher identifies Hwasong district; capture date is not stated. KCNA watermark retained. The source photograph is already in the LOCAL deck; public reuse remains uncleared.
  • Seoul photograph: Laurie Nevay, May 1, 2016, CC BY-SA 2.0. View from Namsan toward central Seoul, despite the local filename’s Gangnam wording. Image displayed without cropping or color alteration.

Delivery

Use the first 35 seconds for the title and brief personal introduction. Advance from the satellite to the two cities, then to the language screen. Model ㄹ in 우리 and 사랑 and allow one audience repetition of each. After the language lesson, advance to the three-part outline for about 20 seconds. Explain Korea at the center of the world story; end the outline with INYEON. Then advance to Words and People. The left arrow reverses these states. Keep this whole opening within two minutes.

Opening pronunciation

In 우리 and 사랑, ㄹ occurs between vowels and is generally a tap. Model it aloud; do not equate it with an English r or an English l. National Institute of Korean Language: international standard Korean curriculum, pronunciation section. The greeting and 우리 meanings retain the earlier language sources.

Getting Korea Right · Words and People

When I say “KOREA”

What words come to mind?

What people?

Older generations

Next generation

Younger generations

Spoken argument · 1½ minutes

When I say “KOREA”, what words come to mind? What people?

For older generations: war. “Police action.” M*A*S*H.

For the next generation: the Olympics. Hyundai. Samsung. LG.

Then Parasite. Squid Game. BTS. K-Dae-Hun—KPop Demon Hunters.

Korea coverage often stays in First Grade: the same scripts repeated endlessly. Second Grade is where the scripts leave off and real knowledge begins.

Those are different Koreas we carry around in our heads. Now let’s look at 한국 and 조선: the South and the North, and the expectations we bring to each.

Delivery

Ask the user-selected Words and People questions and take audience answers before revealing anything. Allow about 30 seconds. Reveal one generation at a time. The Golden button plays the existing 20-second excerpt. Continue to the ROK and DPRK mythbusting.

Sources and supporting detail

Korea changed American power

Evidence and earlier preparation · american-history

Evidence and preparation

The American story often ends with Theodore Roosevelt negotiating peace between Russia and Japan and winning the Nobel Prize. From Korea, the ending looks different. The settlement recognized Japan's dominant position in Korea. A protectorate followed in November 1905; annexation came in 1910. This is not a claim that the treaty itself annexed Korea. It is a reminder that peace between great powers can carry a very different meaning for the people whose future they negotiate.

Sources and media

  • US State Department historian: Treaty of Portsmouth
Evidence and earlier preparation · cold-war

Evidence and preparation

North Korea invaded South Korea in June 1950. The war helped settle the argument in Washington over paying for a large military buildup. These are shares of GDP, not dollar amounts. At the same time, American procurement provided demand for Japanese manufacturers. Toyota's own history describes the military truck orders. Korea was not a peripheral event between World War II and Vietnam. It helped shape the world both countries inhabited afterward.

Sources and media

  • US State Department historian: NSC-68 and spending figures
  • Toyota’s history: Korean War procurement

The Korean War and the defense establishment

U.S. State Department: NSC-68, its adoption, and defense spending as a share of GDP.

Office of the Secretary of Defense history: acquisition and the Korean War buildup. The buildup served broader Cold War purposes, not only the war in Korea.

Eisenhower’s 1961 farewell address. The public phrase is military-industrial complex. Military–industrial–congressional is analytical wording here, not a quotation from that address. The war accelerated an establishment with earlier origins; no single-birth claim is made.

Archival images

Inchon landing, 15 September 1950, NH 42351: photographed from a Marine Air Group Twelve aircraft. Landing craft approach Red Beach; USS De Haven appears below. U.S. Marine Corps / NHHC, public domain. Display crop only.

CIA historical collection: NSC 10/5, 23 October 1951, printed page 437. This is an actual scanned memorandum, not a recreated document. It announces approval of the covert-operations directive; the following pages contain the substantive directive. The cover is an archival illustration, not a photograph of an operation. The CIA was founded in 1947. Badger photograph date is unknown; reactivation date comes from plant history, not the photograph.

National-security state: sources and limits

State Department: NSC-68 and the 5.0% / 14.2% GDP comparison. Korea catalyzed adoption of a global buildup proposed before the invasion. The permanent institutional role is a historical interpretation, not a claim that spending remained at its 1953 peak.

CIA: founded in 1947; Korea was its first hot war. State Department: wartime growth of covert action; NSC 10/5 in October 1951 expanded guerrilla authority. CIA and guerrilla warfare were not created in Korea; greater capacity does not establish operational effectiveness.

Army Environmental Command, Army ammunition production during the Cold War, draft historical report: Badger reactivated March 1951; propellant production resumed under Olin’s Liberty Powder Defense Corporation. Library of Congress HAER WI-8: plant history.

Badger plant photograph: U.S. General Services Administration, public domain. Date unknown; illustrates the site, not verified wartime activity. Original image unchanged, CSS crop only.

South Korea is not our pet

More independent. A stronger ally.

Spoken argument · 4 minutes

South Korea is not going to be our pet forever. It is already a sovereign state, and I expect it to exercise that sovereignty more fully. That does not make it our enemy. To the contrary: a capable ally that chooses to work with us has more to offer.

Look at what Koreans built after the Korean War. Factories, universities, transport systems, and cities under extraordinarily difficult conditions. Overseas assistance and access to markets mattered. So did Korean labor, education, organization, policy, and argument.

Look at the firms Koreans built. This is a dated ranking by market capitalization: the stock market’s value of the company’s shares. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix lead by a long way. Then SK Square, LG Energy Solution, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, and Hyundai Motor. These are separate listed companies, not a ranking of whole business groups. SK Square owns a major stake in SK hynix, so do not add these figures together as if they were separate contributions to the economy. Market value is not annual sales.

Two industries make the result visible: chips and ships. DRAM is working memory used by computers. Worldwide DRAM revenue was $154.73 billion in the second quarter of 2026. Samsung and SK hynix together earned $99.57 billion—64.3 percent of that market. That is revenue in one quarter, not a full year, and one category of memory rather than all semiconductors. Modern computing needs memory as well as processors. Korea belongs inside the story of artificial intelligence.

Korean shipyards build vessels that move energy and goods around the world. South Korea produced about 28 percent of completed commercial gross tonnage in 2024. American efforts to expand shipbuilding now involve Korean investment and expertise.

Those are capabilities America needs. Cooperation includes people on both sides with something valuable to contribute. Korean innovation gives Koreans more influence over the terms of that cooperation.

South Koreans also fought for their democracy. Gwangju in 1980, the movement of 1987, and resistance to the martial-law declaration in December 2024 belong in that history. Citizens, journalists, legislators, and institutions acted. It was not a crisis resolved in one night. Korean society had people prepared to defend its political rights.

Those people have their own views about America, China, Japan, North Korea, and their government’s decisions. We should expect arguments. We should expect governments to change course. Taking Korean democracy seriously means taking those choices seriously.

My expectation is that South Korea will neither do whatever Washington says nor break its American ties. The November 2025 joint agreement reaffirmed the American defense commitment and continued presence of U.S. forces. It also committed both sides to work toward transferring wartime operational control. South Korea seeks greater responsibility for its defense within a continuing alliance.

The investment arrangements included negotiated conditions too. Partnership includes bargaining. The next disagreement belongs in that continuing relationship: security, technology, investment, people, and institutions give both countries reasons to remain engaged. Korean independence and a durable American relationship can develop together.

Delivery

Let the chip and ship images carry the industry examples. The DRAM share is global revenue, Q2 2026; the ship measure is completed commercial gross tonnage, 2024. Do not conflate either with all chips or all maritime activity. Refer to democracy without playing the optional video in the timed talk.

Koreans fought for their democracy

Koreans fought for their democracy

Evidence and earlier preparation · martial-law

Evidence and preparation

This belongs in our account of a global player. On December 3, 2024, President Yoon Suk Yeol declared martial law. Citizens resisted and lawmakers reached the Assembly, which voted 190–0 at 1:02 a.m. on December 4 to demand its end. Yoon announced withdrawal later that morning and the cabinet approved it. Parliament impeached him on December 14; the Constitutional Court removed him on April 4, 2025. These are different steps, not a crisis resolved in one night. Democratic resilience came from people acting and institutions doing their work. Removal did not end political conflict or guarantee future resilience. Americans can learn from Korea’s constitutional experience, too. The 34-second montage restores the original talk’s footage. No autoplay; pause when leaving this slide.

Documentary images and identification

1980: Gwangju street procession. SNU historical photograph collection, attributed there to the May 18 Memorial Foundation. Exact day and photographer not supplied.

1987: Seoul, Gwanggyo demonstration; exact date unknown. Photograph by Jeon Min-jo, National Museum of Contemporary Korean History. Archive image and KOGL Type 1 attribution. Do not assign a specific June date to this image.

2024: Reuters video still, published by The Guardian. Ahn Gwi-ryeong was a Democratic Party spokesperson, not a sitting lawmaker. Reuters interview, December 5, 2024, Jisoo Kim and Daewoung Kim. The confrontation took place during the December 3–4 martial-law night. No claim that she dared the soldier to shoot or that the weapon was loaded.

The Assembly voted 190–0 to demand an end to martial law. On April 4, 2025, the Constitutional Court removed Yoon. Citizens. Parliament. Courts. This was not a crisis resolved in one night. The images show civic action; they do not imply that one person alone ended the crisis. The previous vote-count video is retained in the round 45 backup.

Media use: local editorial presentation only. No open license established for the Gwangju or Reuters images; no public deployment authorized in this revision.

Pie-chart data and dollar values

TrendForce, September 7, 2026: Q2 2026 global DRAM revenue $154.73 billion; Samsung $60.98 billion and 39.4%; SK hynix $38.59 billion and 24.9%. Combined dollars are calculated as 60.98 + 38.59 = 99.57 billion. Combined reported shares are 64.3%; the rest-of-world slice is 35.7%. Shares are rounded; the dollar sum is not obtained by multiplying the rounded percentage. The photograph depicts HBM4, a form of DRAM; the pie covers all DRAM revenue, not just HBM.

UNCTAD Review of Maritime Transport 2025, chapter II: Table II.1, printed p.45, South Korea 28.02% of 2024 completed commercial shipbuilding gross tonnage. Table II.6, printed p.57, world 71,690,983 GT; Korea 20,090,872 GT; rest calculated as 51,600,111 GT. Chart geometry uses 28.02 / 71.98; labels round to 28.0 / 72.0. Scope: deliveries of propelled seagoing merchant ships of 100 GT and above. Gross tonnage measures volume, not weight, number of ships, revenue, orders, or naval output. The report’s prose confirms the 71.7 million GT total despite a misleading thousands-unit table header. UNCTAD Republic of Korea maritime profile independently reports 20,090,872 GT.

Sovereignty and the alliance · wording and sources

“Not our pet” is the speaker’s wording for a relationship that cannot depend on automatic obedience. The Republic of Korea is already a sovereign state. The forecast concerns greater autonomy in practice and greater responsibility for its own defense, not becoming legally sovereign for the first time.

The November 13, 2025 joint fact sheet supports the coexistence of alliance commitments and work toward transferring wartime operational control. The UN member-state record lists the Republic of Korea’s admission on September 17, 1991. “A stronger ally” is the speaker’s interpretation and expectation.

Market capitalization · dated ranking and method

The six firms and values come from StockDigging’s South Korea ranking dated 19 October 2026. It covers KOSPI and KOSDAQ and combines common and preferred shares for each company. Units are trillion South Korean won, without a dollar conversion. The page’s data-source explanation identifies pykrx and NAVER Finance for Korean quotes. StockAnalysis, using S&P Global data, independently gives the same six firms in the same order.

This is a dated provider snapshot, not a claim about final closing prices. Quote-update times differ among sites. Market capitalization changes with share prices. This ranks listed legal entities, not conglomerates. SK Square and its holding SK hynix both appear, so these numbers must not be summed as independent national output.

Getting Korea Right · 한국 / 조선

North Korea is not going to collapse

Production

Deterrence

Support

Adaptation

Kim Ju Ae

3.5% estimated growth in 2025

My forecast · next 10–15 years

In some ways, we can predict a brighter future than the USA’s.

Bank of Korea · July 2026 · Selected images: KCNA / Kremlin (CC BY 4.0) / retained product sources

Spoken argument · 4 minutes

Now the North. I do not expect it to collapse. North Korea survived the loss of its Soviet partner, catastrophic famine, leadership transitions, sanctions, and the pandemic border closure. Waiting for the next crisis to finish it off has repeatedly failed to explain what happened.

Four things help explain its endurance: production, deterrence, external support, and adaptation. Start with production. Look at this new district. Somebody designed these buildings, made the materials, and built them. North Koreans produce housing and consumer goods. Production is a big deal. It belongs in our picture of the country.

The leadership treats nuclear weapons and missiles as protection against outside attack and attempts to remove it. We do not have to endorse that policy to understand the importance it assigns those weapons. Deterrence does not make war impossible. It changes other governments’ choices.

External support matters too. Russia’s war has given North Korea something to supply that a major power wants: weapons and troops. Their treaty and military cooperation give the North additional support and bargaining power. Russia has also obstructed international sanctions monitoring. The North’s international position has changed.

Then adaptation. State ownership and market activity can coexist. Enterprises produce differentiated goods. Shops, showrooms, and licensed markets sell them. Households find ways to earn income and obtain what they need.

Look at the products: shoes, cosmetics, food, bottled drinks, competing beer brands. Someone makes these, sells them, buys them, and judges their quality. Their existence does not tell us that everyone can afford them. It does show economic activity that the picture of an empty, motionless country leaves out.

South Korea’s central bank estimates that the North’s economy grew in 2023, 2024, and 2025. The 2025 estimate is 3.5 percent. Output was still below its 2016 level. Recovery and prosperity are different claims. Photographs of new construction also require evidence about electricity, staffing, supplies, and access.

We need to distinguish the durability of the state from the welfare of its people. Neither darkness in a satellite photograph nor a new apartment tower settles both issues. Production, deterrence, external support, adaptation: together they explain more than the familiar bogeyman on the verge of collapse.

My forecast goes beyond simple survival. In some ways, we can predict a brighter future for North Korea than for the USA. I mean the direction of change over the next ten to fifteen years. I expect North Korea to become stronger and more prominent as American predominance declines. That is a judgment about the future, not a claim that North Koreans are better off today.

Watch Kim Ju Ae. South Korean intelligence regards her as the likely successor. She is still a teenager. We should be paying attention to the next generation of leadership, not waiting for the country to disappear.

Delivery

Use the four mechanisms as the organizing structure. Avoid a product-by-product tour. Let the selected economic evidence support endurance; do not use it as proof of broad prosperity. Sources and fuller galleries remain accessible in supporting material.

New forecast and Kim Ju Ae · evidence and wording

“In some ways, we can predict a brighter future than the USA’s” is the speaker’s qualified comparative forecast, explicitly marked as such on the slide. It is not an observed statistic or a conclusion established by the 3.5% growth estimate. The existing distinction between state power and people’s welfare remains in the spoken argument.

Yonhap, April 6, 2026, directly reports the National Intelligence Service director’s assessment of Kim Ju Ae as the likely successor. AP, September 10, 2026, reports the agency reaffirming that assessment. This is an attributed intelligence assessment, not a formally completed transfer of leadership.

The user called Kim Ju Ae a “Gen Z leader to watch.” The visible wording preserves the future-leadership point as “A young successor to watch.” Her birth year is generally estimated as 2013, but exact details are unconfirmed: Yonhap, January 2, 2026. Generational boundaries also differ; the U.S. Census Bureau’s 2025 cohort report uses 1997–2012 for Gen Z. A categorical Gen Z label would therefore add avoidable uncertainty. She is not presented as the current national leader.

The existing photograph shows her arrival in Beijing in September 2025, credited to KCNA via Chosun/Nate. It is framed toward her in the main-slide layout; the original file and the two-picture supporting slide remain intact. Image provenance · Full supporting photographs. The asset remains for LOCAL review; no open reuse licence was confirmed.

Getting Ourselves Right · 미국

The U.S. and Korea: war, diplomacy, alliance, and enmity

  1. 1871Expedition
  2. 1905Portsmouth
  3. 1945Liberation · division
  4. 1950–53War · armistice · alliance

An alliance in the South. An unfinished conflict with the North.

  1. 1945 · OSSKorean partners against Japan
  2. 1946SSU → CIG / OSOIntelligence operations transferred
  3. 1947 · CIAEarly Cold War

America’s first hot war of the Cold War

U.S. defense outlays · % of GDP

FY 1950≈5%
FY 1953≈14%

Military · Congress · industry · intelligence

National Archives · State Department Historian · OMB historical tables · Photograph: Cpl. Peter McDonald / USMC

132,000Served during the Korean War
801Killed in action
5Medal of Honor recipients

Wisconsin Veterans Museum · Plover memorial · Congressional Medal of Honor Society

Spoken argument · 5 minutes

Now 미국: America. These relationships have a history. Korea governed itself for centuries before it was divided. The Yi royal house lasted from 1392 to 1910, through Joseon and then the Korean Empire. Korea was not waiting for Americans to give it a history.

In 1871, an American expedition fought Korean defenders at Ganghwa. This is the Sujagi, the Korean commanding general’s flag, captured by American forces. The character 帥 means commander. Americans remember an early overseas military action. Koreans remember defending their country.

In 1905, Theodore Roosevelt helped bring Russia and Japan to peace at Portsmouth. Americans remember the Nobel Peace Prize. The settlement recognized Japan’s predominant position in Korea. Koreans had no seat at that table. Japan imposed a protectorate that year; annexation followed in 1910. The same event looks different from Korea.

Liberation from Japanese rule in 1945 brought Soviet occupation in the north and American occupation in the south. American officers proposed the thirty-eighth parallel for accepting Japan’s surrender. The Soviet Union accepted it. Two states followed in 1948. This was not an ancient border separating two different peoples.

The intelligence connection began before the Korean War. In 1945, the Office of Strategic Services—the OSS—trained Korean independence fighters in China for missions against Japan inside Korea. Japan surrendered before the planned wartime infiltration. The anti-Communist phase belongs to the postwar transition. Secret intelligence continued through the Strategic Services Unit, then the Central Intelligence Group and its Office of Special Operations: OSO. The CIA was established in 1947. Korea was one important theater of that transition, not the sole cause of the CIA’s creation.

North Korea invaded the South in June 1950. America’s first hot war of the Cold War helped consolidate a new global order. The United States led the United Nations force. Defense outlays rose from about five percent of GDP in 1950 to fourteen percent in 1953. Intelligence and covert operations expanded rapidly. NATO developed an integrated command. The military, Congress, industry, and intelligence became more tightly connected. These institutions already existed; Korea accelerated their expansion. Wisconsin’s Badger Ordnance Works reopened in 1951. Korean history belongs inside the history of modern American power.

And Korea exposed that power’s limits. The Chinese offensive in November and December 1950 inflicted one of America’s worst military defeats. The Eighth Army retreated in the west; at Chosin in the northeast, Marines fought their way out. This photograph shows that breakout. It was 1950, not December 1951. American leaders had badly underestimated Chinese intervention. U.N. forces recovered, but superior air power, armor, and artillery did not produce unification on American terms. Stalemate followed. American power did not make American judgments correct. That lesson should never be forgotten. That, too, is getting ourselves right.

In July 1953, an armistice stopped the fighting without a final peace settlement. In October, Washington and Seoul signed their mutual defense treaty. South Korea’s president had resisted the armistice and pressed for that alliance. Cooperation never meant agreement on everything. The alliance and the enmity have a history; neither describes all that Koreans are.

Korea is part of Wisconsin’s history. One hundred thirty-two thousand Wisconsinites served during the Korean War. That means service during the war, not that all were sent to Korea. The memorial at Plover records 801 killed in action.

Five Wisconsin men received the Medal of Honor in the Korean War. Here are all five: Stanley Christianson from Mindoro; Melvin Handrich from Manawa; Einar Ingman, born in Milwaukee and later at home in Tomahawk; Mitchell Red Cloud Jr., Ho-Chunk, from Hatfield; and Jerome Sudut from Wausau.

Mitchell Red Cloud Jr. was Ho-Chunk, from Hatfield. Near Chonghyon in November 1950, he warned his company of an approaching attack. Wounded, he kept firing and refused evacuation, giving his company time to organize its defense. He died at twenty-five.

Einar Ingman was born in Milwaukee and came home to Tomahawk. Near Malta-ri in February 1951, he took command of two squads and attacked machine-gun positions despite terrible wounds. He survived and worked at a paper company for thirty-two years. A paper man. In a paper town.

U.S. 51 is Wisconsin’s Korean War Veterans Memorial Highway. Plover’s memorial figures face east, toward Korea. These are Wisconsin families and communities whose history reaches across the Pacific.

Today those alliances and conflicts reach beyond the Pacific. Both Koreas are involved in the war in Europe.

Delivery

Use about one minute for the earlier chronology, two minutes for OSS continuity, the security buildup and the late-1950 reversals, then two minutes for Wisconsin remembrance. Advance twice. Name all five recipients; retain the specific Red Cloud, Ingman, Highway 51 and Plover connections. The photograph is the Chosin breakout, distinct from the Eighth Army’s western-front retreat. The institutional line predates the Korean War; the spending comparison shows its subsequent effect on the United States. Keep the larger claim analytical, not a claim that every institution began in Korea.

Sources and supporting detail

A relationship that is still coming home

Wisconsin remembers

Evidence and earlier preparation · wisconsin-war

Evidence and preparation

North Korea’s invasion of South Korea began the war on June 25, 1950. The United States fought under United Nations command; China later intervened. An armistice stopped the fighting in July 1953 without a final peace treaty. Wisconsin Veterans Museum commemorates 132,000 Wisconsin men and women who served during the war. This does not establish that all were deployed to Korea. Plover’s memorial lists 801 killed in action and 4,286 wounded. We should keep the memorial’s categories explicit, rather than silently treating this as a different total of all wartime deaths. Those relationships live on in veterans and families.

Evidence and earlier preparation · wisconsin-war

Evidence and preparation

North Korea’s invasion of South Korea began the war on June 25, 1950. The United States fought under United Nations command; China later intervened. An armistice stopped the fighting in July 1953 without a final peace treaty. Wisconsin Veterans Museum commemorates 132,000 Wisconsin men and women who served during the war. This does not establish that all were deployed to Korea. Plover’s memorial lists 801 killed in action and 4,286 wounded. We should keep the memorial’s categories explicit, rather than silently treating this as a different total of all wartime deaths. Those relationships live on in veterans and families.

OSS continuity, then the Korean War expansion

Project Eagle in 1945 trained Korean Liberation Army partners in China for intelligence and infiltration against Japan in Korea. Planned wartime deployment was overtaken by surrender. This is not evidence of an OSS war against Korean Communists during World War II. Postwar anti-Communist operations are a separate phase. OSS was dissolved in October 1945; SSU preserved secret-intelligence and counterintelligence functions, transferred to CIG’s Office of Special Operations in 1946. CIA began in September 1947. OSO, not the Air Force’s separate OSI, is the relevant abbreviation here.

The Korean War accelerated an existing national-security system: NSC-68 preceded the invasion, CIA began in 1947, and NATO in 1949. The speaker’s military–congressional–industrial–intelligence formulation is an interpretation of their growing interdependence, not a formal institution founded on one date. NATO approved an integrated command in September 1950; SHAPE began in April 1951.

Budget chart uses rounded national-defense outlays as a percentage of GDP: about 5% in FY1950 and 14% in FY1953. The State Department history gives 5.0% and 14.2%; these match the OMB FY2011 historical-table vintage. All bars share a zero baseline and a 15% maximum. These are total defense outlays, not the cost of fighting in Korea alone.

Late November–December 1950: distinguish the Eighth Army’s Ch’ongch’on/Kunu-ri retreat in the west from X Corps at Chosin and the Hungnam evacuation in the northeast. China’s less heavily equipped ground forces offset U.N. material advantages with tactics, experience, concentration and terrain. U.N. forces subsequently recovered. Negotiations and stalemate followed in 1951–53; the armistice was signed 27 July 1953.

Three Wisconsin figures and all five Korean War recipients

Wisconsin Veterans Museum, Fall 2013 Bugle, printed page 8: 132,000 men and women from Wisconsin served during the Korean War. This is not a count of Wisconsin troops deployed to Korea.

Plover memorial: About the War: 801 killed in action. The page lists deaths in captivity separately. Do not relabel 801 as all war-related deaths.

Historical sequence · 1871, 1905, 1945, 1950–53

Library of Congress country profile, historical background: long Korean institutions, colonial rule, liberation, separate governments in 1948, and the Korean War. The history of Korean self-government precedes division. The Yi royal house continued through the transition from Joseon to the Korean Empire.

State Department historian: Portsmouth: Russia and Japan negotiated their peace with Roosevelt’s mediation. The settlement recognized Japan’s predominant position in Korea. Koreans were not a party to the negotiation. The treaty did not itself annex Korea: the protectorate in 1905 and annexation in 1910 are separate events.

FRUS 1945, volume VI, document 771: Dean Rusk’s 1950 recollection describes the American proposal of the thirty-eighth parallel and Soviet acceptance; the footnote documents the surrender zones in General Order No. 1. Rusk identifies his account as memory, not a reconstruction from documents. The 1945 line is not identical to today’s military demarcation line.

National Archives: original armistice and transcript: signed July 27, 1953, suspending hostilities pending a final peaceful settlement. The military signatories represented United Nations Command, the Korean People’s Army and the Chinese People’s Volunteers. This is distinct from the bilateral alliance treaty.

FRUS: State–Defense instructions of May 30, 1953 document Rhee’s opposition to the proposed armistice and Washington’s offer of mutual-defense negotiations. United Nations Treaty Collection, registration 3363: the U.S.–ROK Mutual Defense Treaty was signed October 1, 1953 and entered into force November 17, 1954. The slide’s 1953 date refers to signature.

The three existing archival photographs have individual captions: Portsmouth in 1905; landing craft at Inchon on September 15, 1950; and Panmunjom on July 27, 1953. None is labeled as a photograph of 1871 or 1945. Their fuller source notes remain in Korean sovereignty history, Korea changed American power, and the armistice discussion The Wisconsin figures, all five portraits, and sources appear in the next reveal.

Late 1950: defeat, retreat, and getting ourselves right

This passage describes the Chinese offensive and the defeat of the U.S. advance in late 1950, including Eighth Army’s defeat in the west. “One of America’s worst military defeats” is a historical characterization, not a numerical ranking. “Single” is deliberately omitted: the fighting around the Ch’ongch’on River and Kunu-ri, the separate Chosin operations, and the ensuing retreat must not be collapsed into one battle.

  • USACE Office of History: the 2d Engineer Combat Battalion at Kunu-ri (March 2001) describes Eighth Army and especially the 2d Infantry Division suffering a resounding defeat in late November 1950. The withdrawal order came on November 29, and the rear-guard disaster on November 30.
  • Air University journal, Spring 2000: review of Stanley Sandler’s The Korean War characterizes the late-1950/early-1951 defeat as “surely one of the worst military defeats ever dealt US forces.” That is the reviewer’s assessment of the campaign, not an official ranked list.
  • Eighth Army’s official history records a 275-mile retreat and calls it the longest in U.S. military history. This distance describes the longer withdrawal into early 1951, not one day or one battle. The same history records recovery and the recapture of Seoul in March 1951.
  • CIA estimate, October 12, 1950, in Foreign Relations of the United States judged full-scale Chinese intervention unlikely in 1950 absent a Soviet decision for global war, while acknowledging it as possible. Naval History and Heritage Command, H-Gram 056 discusses the intelligence failure surrounding the November–December offensive.

The lesson about American power, judgment, and the need to understand other countries is the speaker’s interpretation. It honors the importance of the losses without treating the troops’ courage as proof that senior assessments were sound. This passage does not describe the entire war as one defeat.

Spoken argument · 2½ minutes

Getting the World Right means putting Korea at the center of our understanding. Start with economic scale. South Korea alone is already close to Italy on this measure of GDP: purchasing power, which adjusts for price differences.

A united peninsula would have about seventy-eight million people. If the whole peninsula reached South Korea’s output per person, its economy would be larger than Britain’s, France’s, or Italy’s—still smaller than Germany’s. That is the gold bar. This is a scenario using 2025 population and GDP, not today’s combined output or a promise about unification. Closing that gap would take time and investment.

South Korea is also the world’s ninth-largest major-arms exporter, with three percent of global transfers in 2021–25. This measures delivered military equipment, not dollar sales. Poland was its largest customer. Here are Korean-built K2 tanks in Poland. Korean production is part of European security.

Now look at the war in Europe. Poland builds the Krab howitzer using South Korean K9 chassis technology. The photograph shows one serving in Ukraine. Those three flags show a real connection. On the right are North Korean soldiers training in Russia, in footage released in April 2025. North Korean troops also fought in Russia’s Kursk region. Neither Korea is peripheral here.

My prediction remains: both Koreas become stronger and more prominent over the next ten to fifteen years. Memory, ships, weapons, cultural content: in important areas, I expect their influence to grow relative to Britain, Italy, and Germany. This is broader than a GDP ranking. It is also contingent. South Korea is aging. North Korea faces serious economic limits, and its relationship with Russia can change.

America’s alliance and enemy categories cannot tell us everything we need to know. Both Koreas have capabilities, constraints, and relationships of their own. And here in Neenah, we already have relationships with Korea that go far beyond those categories.

Delivery

Use about 50 seconds for GDP, 25 seconds for the arms-export comparison and 75 seconds for the Europe photographs and forecast. Advance twice. Distinguish PPP from exchange-rate GDP and the conditional convergence scenario from current combined output. The arms chart measures SIPRI transfer volume, not sales revenue. The Krab is Polish-built with South Korean K9 chassis technology. The North Korean photograph shows training in Russia. Save the two-minute discussion of eventual unification for the closing.

Economic scale: observed values and one conditional scenario

Year: 2025. Unit: GDP at purchasing power parity (PPP), current international dollars. World Bank World Development Indicators, last updated 8 October 2026; retrieved 19 October 2026. All solid bars use the same indicator, year and release.

Observed values, trillions: Germany 6.2958; United Kingdom 4.4893; France 4.3964; Italy 3.7001; South Korea 3.2626.

Scenario formula: (South Korea population 51,684,564 + North Korea population 26,571,036) × (South Korea PPP GDP 3,262,583,720,598.03 ÷ South Korea population 51,684,564) = 4,939,878,115,362.09 international dollars, or 4.94 trillion. This assumes equal GDP per person across the peninsula, holding 2025 population and output per person fixed. It is neither a forecast with a target year nor a model of integration costs, institutions, demographics, transition or growth. GDP per person is output per resident, not worker productivity or personal income.

The World Bank GDP series has no comparable DPRK value. A missing value is not zero. The chart does not claim to measure current combined Korean GDP. No Bank of Korea DPRK estimate has been spliced into this comparison.

PPP adjusts for price differences and is useful for comparing domestic output volumes. These are international dollars, not exchange-rate US dollars available to purchase imports. GDP alone does not establish diplomatic or military power.

Measurement sensitivity: at market exchange rates, the same equal-GDP-per-person scenario is US$2.835 trillion. It would exceed Italy (US$2.552T) but remain below France (US$3.366T), the UK (US$4.003T), and Germany (US$5.051T). Do not transfer the PPP rankings to a nominal-dollar claim.

Evidence and earlier preparation · birth-rate

Evidence and preparation

South Korea’s total fertility rate rose from 0.72 in 2023 to 0.75 in 2024 and 0.80 in 2025. This is a modest rise, not a new record low. Total fertility rate summarizes a year’s age-specific birth rates: it is not the completed family size of today’s young women, not a prediction that each woman will have 0.80 children. About 2.1 is a replacement benchmark for a low-mortality population without migration; it does not predict a population’s near-term size. Wisconsin is not at the same fertility level. But our Department of Workforce Development also identifies an aging population as a challenge for worker availability. Care, work and family life connect the two stories. The preceding robot slide shows one technological capacity, not proof that low fertility caused Korea’s robot adoption.

INYEON · A connection shaped by encounters and time

Yuhan-Kimberly

29th floor

Huggies · Kleenex · Kotex

Spoken argument · 2 minutes

인연. Inyeon. A connection or bond. It has a history: people meet, work together, and become part of one another’s lives. Wisconsin and Korea have more of that history than you might think.

This is Lotte World Tower in Seoul: 555 meters tall. On the twenty-ninth floor is the headquarters of a company with a familiar connection: Yuhan-Kimberly.

Kimberly-Clark began here in Neenah in 1872. In 1970, it joined with the Korean company Yuhan. More than fifty years of making products for Korean families. Huggies. Kleenex. Kotex.

Some of you probably worked on that relationship.

From a paper mill on the Fox River to the Seoul skyline. A connection with names, dates, products, and people behind it. The headquarters is in Songpa-gu. That is where this Wisconsin connection has a place in contemporary Seoul.

The Fox River and Seoul belong in the same story. And Kimberly-Clark is only the beginning of our Wisconsin connections.

Getting the World Right · 인연

Wisconsin works with Korea

Yuhan-Kimberly

FY2025 worldwide sales

Madison / Seoul

Lab instruments

Hsu’s · Marathon County

Korean ginseng grown here, says Hsu’s

Oshkosh + Hanwha

2021 · Army vehicle concept award

2023 · Other teams selected

Wisconsin–Korea goods · 2025

$724M to Korea

$472M from Korea

Company totals, not Wisconsin–Korea trade.

Spoken argument · 3 minutes

Here are companies and actual products. These sales figures tell us the size of the businesses. They are company totals, not the amount each company sells between Wisconsin and Korea.

Yuhan-Kimberly, the connection we just saw, reported 1.40 trillion won in sales in 2025. About ninety percent of its sales were domestic. Diapers, tissues, and other everyday products connect Kimberly-Clark’s Neenah history with Korean households.

Doosan Bobcat reported $6.18 billion in worldwide revenue in 2025. In Johnson Creek, it makes mowers and grounds equipment. Its parent headquarters is in Korea. The equipment looks perfectly at home on a Wisconsin property. Korean ownership and Wisconsin manufacturing are already working together.

Rockwell Automation reported $8.34 billion in worldwide sales for its 2025 fiscal year. Here are its factory controllers. Its headquarters is in Milwaukee, and its customer experience center in Seoul brings industrial automation to Korean customers.

Madison-based Promega has a Seoul operation that develops and manufactures the Maxwell instrument line. It is privately held and does not publish its financial statements. Scientific work in Wisconsin and Korea belongs to the same business.

And Hsu’s needs an explanation. The company says it grows Korean ginseng from Korean seed on its Wisconsin farms. That is a specific connection. It does not establish how much Hsu’s sells to Korea. Wisconsin’s main ginseng crop is American ginseng, a different species; China and Hong Kong are its principal overseas markets. Marathon County grows about 95 percent of Wisconsin’s crop.

Then Oshkosh Defense and Hanwha. They worked together on an Army vehicle concept in 2021. The Army selected other teams for the next phases in 2023. The collaboration was real, and so was that outcome. An American manufacturer saw Korean engineering as something worth working with.

Across all companies, Wisconsin exported about $724 million in goods to South Korea and imported about $472 million in 2025. Medical and scientific instruments, machinery, food, meat and dairy are part of that exchange. Scientists, factory workers, engineers, and farmers are part of the relationship. Wisconsin contributes things Korea values. Korea contributes things Wisconsin values.

Delivery

Begin with the three products, logos, Wisconsin places, and sales figures. Explain once that these are total company sales, not bilateral trade. Yuhan-Kimberly is shown in Korean won; the other two amounts are U.S. dollars. Advance once to Promega, Hsu’s, and Oshkosh–Hanwha, with the Wisconsin–Korea goods totals below them. Explain Hsu’s cultivation claim; do not call it a proven exporter to Korea. Both reveals belong to this one three-minute slide.

Fermented cabbage

Love our underdogs

Hitting high above our weight.

Four seasons. Work hard. Play hard.

정Affection and closeness

Two residential settings · Different dates and camera scales

Spoken argument · 2 minutes

Put Wisconsin and Korea at the same map scale. Both Koreas together have about thirteen times Wisconsin’s population. South Korea’s economy alone was about four times Wisconsin’s in 2024. Seoul is closer to San Francisco’s latitude than Madison’s. Distance does not make Korea small. Now look at what feels familiar.

What do Korea and Wisconsin have in common? Start with fermented cabbage: sauerkraut and kimchi. Different tastes, familiar traditions.

Four seasons. We work hard, we play hard, and we love our underdog sports teams. These are things I recognize in both places. We have more in common than we might think. And both Wisconsin and Korea hit high above their weight: paper, machinery, chips, ships, and culture.

Wisconsin has its traditions of hospitality and Gemütlichkeit. Korean has 정, jeong: affection and closeness. Those are different words with different histories. But we can recognize the pleasure of eating together, making someone welcome, and getting to know them over time.

Here are two residential settings: West Allis and Suwon. These photographs do not stand for every home in Wisconsin or South Korea. One shows houses and yards; the other, apartment towers and shared grounds. We can recognize homes while noticing very different arrangements of space. Understanding Korea means being able to hold both things in mind: the resemblance and the difference.

That is the human part of 인연. We already have relationships through work, war, families, and paper. We can add friendship. We can visit, learn, and invest in one another. And that brings us to the future.

Getting the World Right · 인연 · INYEON

An imagined Seoul · KPop Demon Hunters

Korea is a live player.

The U.S.–Korea relationship has been and will be important.

Wisconsin has good inyeon to build on.

친구friend CHINGU

Spoken argument · 4 minutes

인연 has a past. It also has a future. This is an imagined Korean future. We have spent a long time seeing Korea through war, division, and expectations of collapse. We can also imagine what Koreans may build.

Here are my predictions for the next ten to fifteen years. Stronger Koreas. A South that makes more of its own decisions and remains our ally. A North that keeps producing and building. In important areas, I expect Korean influence to grow relative to Britain, Italy, and Germany.

For America, I expect less dominance and more need for Korean partners. For Wisconsin, especially the Fox Valley, I expect more Korean connections: trade, investment, and people. We already have the relationships and capabilities to build on. It will take work to make those opportunities real.

Perhaps, eventually, Korea/Joseon. I expect the possibility of Korean unification to increase as American predominance declines. A more capable South Korea may seek greater freedom to arrange its own security. Changes in outside support and pressure can change what both Korean governments consider possible. Arrangements that once appeared fixed could become negotiable.

That is a possibility, not a timetable. I am not putting unification on a fifteen-year schedule. An armistice stopped the fighting in 1953 without a final peace settlement. Division has lasted a long time, but duration alone does not decide every part of the future.

China would have a strong interest in the outcome. So would the United States. Koreans would have to make and sustain the agreement. Neither outside power can supply the trust that requires. Korean innovation and greater capability can create more room for Korean decisions, but they do not by themselves produce an agreement.

There are serious obstacles. The North’s leadership has moved toward treating the South as a hostile separate state. Both governments have institutions and interests bound up with division. A change in the balance of power could reinforce that division as well as loosen it. Peace, renewed contact, and practical cooperation have value before unification. We should be able to consider these possibilities without waiting for the North to disappear.

One possibility for us: Neenah and Jeonju, sister cities through paper. Our paper heritage and Jeonju’s living hanji tradition. Friendship, exchange, and investment.

Yuhan-Kimberly, Promega, Bobcat, Rockwell, Oshkosh and Hanwha, Wisconsin ginseng. Veterans and their families. Students and teachers. We already have inyeon. We can make more of it.

We began with 우리 and 사랑. We have also learned 정, the affection and closeness that grow as people know one another. Getting Korea Right, Getting Ourselves Right, Getting the World Right.

The next time Korea makes the news, you’re ready for Second Grade: where the scripts leave off and real knowledge begins.

When you follow Korea, you're ahead of the world.

Keep learning. Keep trading. Keep building together. Thank you.

Korea is a live player. The U.S.–Korea relationship has been and will be important. Wisconsin has good inyeon to build on. Inyeon: a connection shaped by encounters and time. 친구 means friend. CHINGU.

Delivery and sources

Allow 0:00–0:20 for the imagined future. Advance to the forecasts for 0:20–1:00. Keep this final view for the two-minute Korea/Joseon discussion, 1:00–3:00. Use 3:00–4:00 for the brief paper proposal, the Wisconsin connections, and the closing lines. There is no separate “Our future connection” screen. The three-part outline ends with INYEON; the spoken talk ends with CHINGU. Return to the Second Grade objective before the closing theme. Keep eventual unification and the proposed sister-city relationship distinct from the 10–15-year forecast. Say “Thank you” before the final Korean word. Finish with CHINGU and pause.

“Stronger Koreas” is the speaker’s forecast for the next 10–15 years. “Perhaps, eventually, Korea/Joseon” is a possibility beyond that forecast, not a promised date or political formula. North Korea’s hostile two-state policy remains a serious obstacle; the full armistice and unification discussion remains in supporting material.

The Neenah–Jeonju sister-city relationship is a proposal, not a claim that an agreement already exists. Jeonju’s Millennium Hanji Center preserves, transmits, and promotes traditional handmade paper. The city also documents its Hanji Museum. Photograph provenance.

Jeonju and Cheongju are different cities. The user selected Jeonju for the future paper relationship. Jikji was printed in Cheongju in 1377; that object and the printing history remain visible in supporting material. The forecast’s evidence and the original paper history are retained below.

Sources and supporting detail

A paper town can build another connection

In a paper town, start with paper

Evidence and earlier preparation · jikji

Evidence and preparation

This is Jikji, a Buddhist text printed in Cheongju. The surviving metal-type volume is in the National Library of France. It does not mean that all later European printing descended from Korea; that is a different historical claim. It means that a familiar story of technological invention is incomplete when Korea is left out. Korea's present capabilities have a history. We should not reduce the entire country to a recent miracle of catching up.

Sources and media

  • BnF: Jikji, 1377
  • Original paper, printing and Buddhist-history material

A future connection for the Fox Valley

Evidence and earlier preparation · neenah

Evidence and preparation

Inyeon means connections formed through people, encounters and time. Here is ours: Kimberly-Clark, founded in Neenah in 1872, joined Yuhan in 1970. Some of you probably worked on that relationship. Yuhan-Kimberly’s headquarters is on the 29th floor of Lotte World Tower. We are not introducing two strangers. We are recognizing an old connection. The tower is in Songpa; the Gangnam Style association is cultural, not a claim about its district.

Getting Korea Right, Getting Ourselves Right, Getting the World Right

Getting Korea Right, Getting Ourselves Right, Getting the World Right

Evidence and earlier preparation · rogers

Evidence and preparation

Jim Rogers has made a bullish case for a unified Korea. This is a dated quotation from 2018, not a new forecast. He emphasized the combination of the South's capital and know-how with the North's people, resources and location. His confidence is an investor's thesis, not proof that political barriers will disappear. My use of 'long Korea' is broader: invest attention, knowledge and relationships in a place whose importance we still underestimate. Rogers is one investor with a dated formulation of that possibility. The point is to invest attention and relationships in Korea already, rather than waiting for unification.

Sources and media

  • Aju News: actual January 2018 interview
Evidence and earlier preparation · closing

Evidence and preparation

Return to Neenah. We began with a relationship already made: companies, families, service and work. Understanding Korea helps us understand how that relationship came to be and what it might become. Getting Korea right, getting ourselves right, getting the world right. Thank you.

    Religious traditions

    Evidence and earlier preparation · faith

    Evidence and preparation

    Jikji is a Buddhist text. That takes us from printing to people and their traditions. Buddhist temples, Confucian family and ancestral rites, and shamanic ritual all belong in our account of Korea. These are not three exclusive boxes, and they are not the whole religious landscape. Christianity and people with no religious affiliation are major parts of South Korean society. Coexistence does not mean an absence of conflict or persecution. My own Wisconsin–Korea connection includes translating Korean Buddhist teachers and teaching at Lawrence University in Appleton. Religion belongs in this talk because it is part of lived Korea—and part of my relationship with it.

    Seoul tourism and the film

    Seoul Metropolitan Government reported record July 2025 arrivals, 1.36 million, and attributed additional tourism momentum to KPop Demon Hunters. No verified worldwide fastest-growth ranking is asserted. Visit Seoul identifies Namsan Seoul Tower as a location depicted in the film.

    Seoul Metropolitan Government, September 2025 · Visit Seoul: Namsan Seoul Tower

    Future Wisconsin–Korea connections: evidence and forecast

    The forecast of deeper Wisconsin–Korea ties is the speaker’s judgment, conditional on people and institutions developing the opportunities. The existing company relationships establish a basis for cooperation. They do not establish future investment commitments, contracts or job totals.

    The U.S. Dairy Export Council’s September 17, 2025 supplier showcase in Madison brought buyers from Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong together with U.S. suppliers. This is a documented Wisconsin trade connection, not a Fox Valley-specific investment announcement. WEDC’s trade-mission program provides one established route to developing business relationships.

    Jeonju’s Millennium Hanji Center documents papermaking education, crafts and restoration research. These activities provide concrete possible subjects for a paper exchange. No Neenah–Jeonju agreement or funded exchange is claimed.

    Greater Korean influence relative to Britain, Italy and Germany concerns capabilities and strategic weight in particular areas. It is not a forecast of a single GDP ranking. The ROK already is sovereign; the forecast concerns greater freedom of action. The U.S. relative-power forecast and the proposed relationship between that change and unification are the speaker’s interpretation, not a demonstrated causal law.

    Words for our connection

    안녕하세요

    annyeonghaseyo

    Hello

    우리

    uri

    We / our

    인연

    inyeon

    Connection / bond

    Spoken argument · 1 minute

    Try these with me. 안녕하세요. Annyeonghaseyo. Hello. 우리. Uri. We or our. 인연. Inyeon. A connection or bond formed through encounters.

    Inyeon is a good word for what we have just seen. People encounter one another, work together, and develop a relationship with a history. A name on a building gives us a way into that history.

    We have other ways of recognizing one another. Coleslaw at a fish fry, sauerkraut in Wisconsin’s German heritage, kimchi at a Korean meal. Gemütlichkeit and jeong are different traditions, but both help us talk about warmth and attachment.

    Getting Korea right begins with recognizing a relationship we already have. The Fox River and Seoul belong in the same story. And Kimberly-Clark is only the beginning of our Wisconsin connections.

    Delivery

    Model each Korean word and allow one repetition, totaling about 12 seconds. Romanization is a reading aid; let the speaker model the sound. Uri can mean we or our. Inyeon names a relationship, tie or connection; it does not always imply predestination.

    Language sources

    Retained vocabulary notes and source links. The three terms, romanizations and meanings are retained from the previous Neenah slide.

    The images we inherited

    “Fish for, crush, or film”

    Supporting explanation

    We inherited some powerful images of Korea. Here it is in an old cartoon, something for other powers to fish for. Here it is being crushed between them. And then M*A*S*H: Korea as the setting for an American story.

    For a century Korea has been the thing other people fish for, crush, or film. Those images can make it hard to see Koreans doing things themselves.

    Korea is already part of American life

    30%

    Samsung · U.S. smartphone shipments
    Q2 2026

    10.8%

    U.S. new-vehicle sales · 2025
    Excludes Genesis

    Parasite · Squid Game
    BTS · BLACKPINK

    Shipments and new sales, not installed shares · Counterpoint / manufacturers / Wards · KPop Demon Hunters: American production, Korean cultural influence · Netflix / Sony

    Supporting explanation

    But Korea is already in American life. Samsung and LG in our homes. Hyundai and Kia on our roads. Korean components inside products carrying other countries’ brands.

    Then Parasite, Squid Game, BTS, BLACKPINK. KPop Demon Hunters is an American production drawing on Korean culture and an international team. Korean influence reaches us through Hollywood too.

    Your grandchildren may recognize some of these connections faster than we do. The encounter is already happening. And here in Neenah, we have a connection of our own.

    Evidence and earlier preparation · culture

    Evidence and preparation

    Some of us first met Korea through the war or through M*A*S*H. A younger generation encounters Korean music, Korean storytelling and Korean settings without needing an introduction. These examples are different kinds of production: KPop Demon Hunters is a Sony Pictures Animation film released by Netflix, shaped by Korean culture and international collaboration. The point is global influence, not that every production here was made by a Korean company. Play a short section of Golden, then continue. Use the button for a twenty-second excerpt, 0:45–1:05; leaving this slide stops the player. This turns recognition into a brief shared experience. Streaming needs internet.

    Wisconsin and Korea: familiar latitude, different scale

    13×

    Wisconsin’s population

    Both Koreas · 2024
    4.1×

    Wisconsin’s economy

    South Korea · 2024 nominal GDP

    Madison 43.1°N · Seoul 37.6°N · San Francisco 37.8°N

    Population: Census / World Bank · GDP: BEA / World Bank · North Korean population estimated

    Supporting explanation

    First, put Korea beside Wisconsin. Each Korean state has less land than Wisconsin. Together, they have about seventy-eight million people: thirteen Wisconsins. South Korea’s economy is about four times Wisconsin’s.

    Seoul is south of Madison, almost at San Francisco’s latitude. Korea is a concentrated part of the world, with a scale we can compare to places we know.

That older total-area comparison is retained here as supporting evidence, not as the basis of this map or density calculation.

    Evidence and earlier preparation · population

    Evidence and preparation

    Wisconsin is the scale we know. South Korea alone has about 8.7 times our population; both Koreas together have about 13.1 times. Census Wisconsin July 1, 2024 estimate: 5,957,168, revised series. World Bank midyear population estimates: South Korea 51,751,065 and North Korea 26,498,823. These are estimates for a common year, not identical national census exercises.

    A relationship that is still coming home

    132,000

    Wisconsinites served
    during the war

    801

    Killed in action
    Plover memorial count

    Charles A. Dickman · Cashton

    17 years old · missing in 1950

    Accounted for and home in 2023

    More than seventy years later

    Wisconsin Korean War Veterans Memorial · Korean War Veterans Memorial Highway · DPAA / U.S. Army

    Supporting explanation

    For many Wisconsin families, the relationship begins with the war. The memorial at Plover records 132,000 Wisconsinites who served during the Korean War and 801 killed in action. Service during the war and the memorial’s record of those killed are different categories. They represent families across this state.

    U.S. 51 is Wisconsin’s Korean War Veterans Memorial Highway. The figures at Plover face east, toward Korea.

    Charles A. Dickman, from Cashton, was seventeen when he went missing in July 1950. His remains were accounted for in 2023. That October, his family finally buried him at home. More than seventy years later.

    Sources and supporting detail

    Wisconsin remembers

    Evidence and earlier preparation · wisconsin-war

    Evidence and preparation

    North Korea’s invasion of South Korea began the war on June 25, 1950. The United States fought under United Nations command; China later intervened. An armistice stopped the fighting in July 1953 without a final peace treaty. Wisconsin Veterans Museum commemorates 132,000 Wisconsin men and women who served during the war. This does not establish that all were deployed to Korea. Plover’s memorial lists 801 killed in action and 4,286 wounded. We should keep the memorial’s categories explicit, rather than silently treating this as a different total of all wartime deaths. Those relationships live on in veterans and families.

    Sources

    • Wisconsin Korean War Veterans Memorial · Plover
    • Wisconsin Veterans Museum: 132,000 served during the war
    • National Archives: Korean armistice
    • Wisconsin DOT: U.S. 51 designation
    • Memorial design and family stories

    U.S. 51 is Wisconsin’s Korean War Veterans Memorial Highway, designated in 1987. The original memorial page preserves the design’s east-facing figures and other memorial details. Its 84 missing-person figure dates to the 1993 dedication, not a current count.

    Evidence and earlier preparation · charles-dickman

    Evidence and preparation

    The original memorial page included Charles Dickman. DPAA identified his remains after earlier burial as an unknown soldier in Hawaii. The Army documented his October 2023 burial in Cashton. His story gives a specific meaning to remembrance continuing across generations. Do not confuse him with Ingman: Dickman returned as identified remains, not as a living veteran.

    Wisconsin lives on both sides of the map

    A paper man.
    In a paper town.

    Five Wisconsin recipients: Stanley Christianson · Melvin Handrich · Einar Ingman · Mitchell Red Cloud Jr. · Jerome Sudut

    Malta-ri approximate · Plover and Neenah marked for Wisconsin context · Wisconsin Veterans Museum

    Supporting explanation

    Five Wisconsin-connected Medal of Honor recipients: Stanley Christianson, Melvin Handrich, Einar Ingman, Mitchell Red Cloud Jr., and Jerome Sudut. I want to spend a moment with two of them.

    Mitchell Red Cloud Jr. was Ho-Chunk, from Hatfield. In November 1950, near Chonghyon, in what is now North Korea, he saw a Chinese attack approaching and sounded the alarm. Wounded, he continued firing and refused evacuation. His actions gave his company time to organize its defense. He died at twenty-five.

    Einar Ingman was born in Milwaukee and came home to Tomahawk. In February 1951, near Malta-ri, he took command of two squads and attacked two machine-gun positions despite terrible wounds. He survived. Then he worked at a paper company for thirty-two years.

    A paper man. In a paper town.

    Sources and supporting detail

    Names and hometowns

    Evidence and earlier preparation · wisconsin-people

    Evidence and preparation

    These are places you know. Mitchell Red Cloud Jr., a Ho-Chunk soldier from Hatfield, was killed in action in November 1950. Einar Ingman survived extraordinary wounds in February 1951 and returned to Wisconsin. He later worked in a paper mill. A paper man. In a paper town. Korea is part of Wisconsin's history through particular people, not only through a treaty or a trade figure. Both men received the Medal of Honor for actions in the Korean War. These are two Wisconsin stories, not a claim that Wisconsin had only two recipients.

    Korea changed American power

    U.S. defense spending / GDP

    1950
    5.0%
    1953
    14.2%

    Wisconsin propellants · American institutions · Japanese industry, including Toyota

    Supporting explanation

    The war also changed Wisconsin’s work. Badger Ordnance Works reopened in 1951 to make propellants. Across the United States, military spending and the national-security establishment expanded. American wartime procurement helped rebuild Japanese industry too, including Toyota.

    Korea belongs in the history of how modern American power was built. Getting Korea right changes how we understand ourselves.

    Sources and supporting detail

    Korea changed American power

    Evidence and earlier preparation · american-history

    Evidence and preparation

    The American story often ends with Theodore Roosevelt negotiating peace between Russia and Japan and winning the Nobel Prize. From Korea, the ending looks different. The settlement recognized Japan's dominant position in Korea. A protectorate followed in November 1905; annexation came in 1910. This is not a claim that the treaty itself annexed Korea. It is a reminder that peace between great powers can carry a very different meaning for the people whose future they negotiate.

    Sources and media

    • US State Department historian: Treaty of Portsmouth
    Evidence and earlier preparation · cold-war

    Evidence and preparation

    North Korea invaded South Korea in June 1950. The war helped settle the argument in Washington over paying for a large military buildup. These are shares of GDP, not dollar amounts. At the same time, American procurement provided demand for Japanese manufacturers. Toyota's own history describes the military truck orders. Korea was not a peripheral event between World War II and Vietnam. It helped shape the world both countries inhabited afterward.

    Sources and media

    • US State Department historian: NSC-68 and spending figures
    • Toyota’s history: Korean War procurement

    The Korean War and the defense establishment

    U.S. State Department: NSC-68, its adoption, and defense spending as a share of GDP.

    Office of the Secretary of Defense history: acquisition and the Korean War buildup. The buildup served broader Cold War purposes, not only the war in Korea.

    Eisenhower’s 1961 farewell address. The public phrase is military-industrial complex. Military–industrial–congressional is analytical wording here, not a quotation from that address. The war accelerated an establishment with earlier origins; no single-birth claim is made.

    Archival images

    Inchon landing, 15 September 1950, NH 42351: photographed from a Marine Air Group Twelve aircraft. Landing craft approach Red Beach; USS De Haven appears below. U.S. Marine Corps / NHHC, public domain. Display crop only.

    CIA historical collection: NSC 10/5, 23 October 1951, printed page 437. This is an actual scanned memorandum, not a recreated document. It announces approval of the covert-operations directive; the following pages contain the substantive directive. The cover is an archival illustration, not a photograph of an operation. The CIA was founded in 1947. Badger photograph date is unknown; reactivation date comes from plant history, not the photograph.

    National-security state: sources and limits

    State Department: NSC-68 and the 5.0% / 14.2% GDP comparison. Korea catalyzed adoption of a global buildup proposed before the invasion. The permanent institutional role is a historical interpretation, not a claim that spending remained at its 1953 peak.

    CIA: founded in 1947; Korea was its first hot war. State Department: wartime growth of covert action; NSC 10/5 in October 1951 expanded guerrilla authority. CIA and guerrilla warfare were not created in Korea; greater capacity does not establish operational effectiveness.

    Army Environmental Command, Army ammunition production during the Cold War, draft historical report: Badger reactivated March 1951; propellant production resumed under Olin’s Liberty Powder Defense Corporation. Library of Congress HAER WI-8: plant history.

    Badger plant photograph: U.S. General Services Administration, public domain. Date unknown; illustrates the site, not verified wartime activity. Original image unchanged, CSS crop only.

    2025 · goods

    Medical / scientific instruments · machinery · food and dairy

    WEDC · rounded goods flows · Promega, Doosan Bobcat and Rockwell are documented examples, not a ranked top three

    Supporting explanation

    The relationship continued through trade. In 2025, Wisconsin exported about $724 million in goods to South Korea and imported about $472 million. Medical and scientific instruments, machinery, food, meat and dairy are part of that exchange.

    Doosan Bobcat has its parent headquarters in Korea and makes mowers and grounds equipment in Johnson Creek. Madison-based Promega has a Seoul operation developing and manufacturing its Maxwell instrument line. Milwaukee-based Rockwell Automation operates a customer experience center in Seoul.

    These are specific connections between skills, equipment, and people.

    Wisconsin contributes, too

    Ginseng

    Wisconsin grows nearly all U.S. commercial ginseng. Hsu’s says it also grows Korean ginseng on its Wisconsin farms. American and Korean ginseng are different species.

    Engineering

    2021 · Army concept-design award
    2023 · Other teams selected for next phases

    Ginseng: Marathon City · Royalbroil, 2007 · CC BY-SA 2.5 · Redback: Australian configuration · collaboration is not a production-contract win

    Supporting explanation

    Oshkosh Defense worked with Hanwha on an Army vehicle concept in 2021. The Army selected other teams for the next phases in 2023. The collaboration was real, and so was that outcome. It tells us something about Korean capabilities an American manufacturer wanted to work with.

    Another connection grows in Marathon County: ginseng. Wisconsin grows nearly all of America’s commercial crop. Hsu’s says it grows Korean ginseng from Korean seed on its Wisconsin farms. That is a specific cultivation connection, not evidence of a sales total to Korea. Wisconsin’s main American-ginseng export markets are China and Hong Kong.

    Wisconsin contributes agricultural and engineering knowledge to these relationships. We have been working together for a long time.

    Sources and supporting detail

    Ginseng · Marathon County

    Evidence and earlier preparation · wisconsin-ginseng

    Evidence and preparation

    Ginseng belongs in this talk alongside chips and ships. Wisconsin grows American ginseng; Korean ginseng is a different species. The state agriculture department currently says almost 98% of US production comes from Wisconsin, with Marathon County producing about 95% of the state crop. Earlier drafts used 90–95%; this slide uses the stable phrase nearly all. Korea’s long association with ginseng creates a familiar cultural and commercial connection, not proof that Korea buys most Wisconsin production. The original tariff comparison is preserved in the original slide, explicitly a 2012 KORUS base schedule; 754% must not be presented as today’s tariff.

    Trade context, product photographs and Hsu’s

    WEDC 2025 full-year report, export table page 4: China $1,018,247,129; Japan $735,796,635; South Korea $723,657,401. Import table page 10: South Korea $471,804,303. The three countries are selected comparisons, not Wisconsin’s top three. All values are goods flows, not services or individual-company sales. Exports use Census origin of movement; imports use state of destination. They do not prove where every product was manufactured or ultimately consumed. Do not calculate a state trade balance from these totals.

    Product images identify Wisconsin–Korea businesses and their products; they are not evidence that the pictured units were shipped from Wisconsin to Korea. Promega’s Maxwell instruments are manufactured by its Seoul operation. Bobcat’s pictured mowing location is unidentified. Rockwell’s image shows ControlLogix controllers, not a specific Korean shipment.

    Hsu’s Korean Red Ginseng product description states that the company selects Korean ginseng seeds and cultivates them on its Wisconsin farms. This is a company-attributed cultivation claim, not verified Hsu’s export revenue. No company-to-Korea sales amount was found. Wisconsin DATCP supplies the broader Wisconsin and Marathon County production context. Ginseng Board submission, October 17, 2024, reports that about 85% of the crop is exported, primarily to China and Hong Kong. No current Korean tariff is inferred here.

    1905 / 1910Protectorate / annexation

    1945 / 1948Occupation / two states

    Supporting explanation

    Working together requires understanding why Koreans insist on making their own choices. The Yi royal house governed from 1392 until 1910, through Joseon and then the Korean Empire. More than five centuries of institutions, scholarship, arguments, and adaptation.

    Long continuity did not mean uninterrupted peace. Japan invaded in 1592, seeking to conquer Korea and advance into China. Admiral Yi Sun-sin’s naval victories disrupted Japanese supply lines. Ming China intervened. Koreans fought for their country in a regional struggle.

    In 1905, Japan and Russia negotiated peace at Portsmouth, New Hampshire. Theodore Roosevelt won the Nobel Peace Prize for his mediation. The settlement recognized Japan’s predominance in Korea. Koreans had no seat at that table. Japan imposed a protectorate that year and annexed Korea in 1910.

    Liberation in 1945 brought Soviet occupation in the north and American occupation in the south. American officers proposed the thirty-eighth parallel, and the Soviet Union accepted it. Two separate states followed in 1948. That border did not come from an ancient Korean division.

    Koreans have a long experience of governing themselves, and a painful experience of other powers deciding for them. That helps explain why cooperation with America can be deeply valued without every American demand being accepted.

    Sources and supporting detail

    Long continuity. Repeated invasion.

    Korean sovereignty

    Portsmouth photograph and historical documentation remain in the following American power slide’s preserved source notes. See also the original Portsmouth discussion.

    1945: the occupation line

    FRUS, 1945, volume VI, document 771: Dean Rusk’s July 1950 recollection of the August 1945 proposal. Rusk names himself and Charles H. Bonesteel III; the 38th parallel divided responsibility for accepting Japanese surrender. Rusk explicitly describes his account as memory rather than a reconstruction from documents. The document’s footnote also describes General Order No. 1.

    State Department historical overview: occupation in 1945; two states in 1948. The 1945 parallel is not identical to the present military demarcation line. The division’s later consolidation involved Soviet, American and Korean decisions; the proposal alone did not mechanically determine every subsequent event.
